hints: Remember adult haemoglobin has four globin subunits made up of two kinds, with two copies of each kind - think which Greek letters are used to label the two kinds.
walkthrough:
Recall the 2 x 2 subunit model**
Adult haemoglobin is a classic quaternary structure protein with four polypeptides. They are not all identical. There are two copies of one type and two copies of another type, packed together.

Name the two types**
The two types are the alpha globin chains and the beta globin chains, so one molecule is $\alpha_2\beta_2$. The different shading in Fig. 3.1 shows these two populations.
Final answer: alpha (globin) chain and beta (globin) chain.

hints: Look closely at label P - it points to a small non-polypeptide structure tucked inside the folded globin, not the coiled ribbon itself. Think what iron-containing part sits in each subunit to handle oxygen.
walkthrough:
Separate protein from non-protein**
Each globin chain folds around a small non-amino acid part. That is why P looks like sticks rather than a ribbon coil. It is a prosthetic group, meaning a non-protein permanently associated with the protein.

Identify P**
In each of the four subunits that group is haem, containing $Fe^{2+}$, which provides the actual binding site for one $O_2$ molecule. So one haemoglobin can carry four $O_2$ in total.
Final answer: haem (prosthetic group).

hints: Work up through the levels from smallest to largest - sequence of amino acids, then alpha-helix, then 3D folding of one chain, then assembly of four chains. Which level is too small to see in this 3D ribbon model?
walkthrough:
Map what you can see**
The coils are alpha-helices, so secondary structure is visible. The 3D folding of each globin is tertiary structure. The packing of four subunits together is quaternary structure.

Spot what is missing**
What you cannot read off is the exact order of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. That sequence is primary structure, which determines all the higher levels of folding.
Final answer: primary structure - sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide.

hints: Start by separating the two CO2 routes in the red cell. Most CO2 becomes carbonic acid and hydrogencarbonate ions, but focus here only on CO2 that stays as CO2 - think how it could be carried directly on haemoglobin.
Think about where on the globin polypeptide CO2 can attach. It does not go on the iron in haem, but on a nitrogen-containing group at the ends of the polypeptide chains.
Recall the name given to haemoglobin once CO2 is bound this way, and think where in the body this compound must split apart again when $pCO_2$ is low and $pO_2$ is high.
walkthrough:
Direct binding, not via carbonic acid**
In respiring muscle, CO2 diffuses into red blood cells. A proportion binds directly to haemoglobin itself rather than reacting with water. Think of haemoglobin acting as a carrier for CO2 as well as for oxygen.

Forming carbaminohaemoglobin**
CO2 reacts with terminal amine groups ($-NH_2$) of the globin polypeptide chains. This forms a compound called carbaminohaemoglobin. It is a reversible combination, not the same as oxygen binding to haem iron.

Release in the lungs**
Blood carries this to a region of low $pCO_2$ and high $pO_2$, the pulmonary capillaries around the alveoli. There carbaminohaemoglobin dissociates, releasing CO2 to diffuse out into the alveolar air for exhalation.

Final answer: CO2 binds directly to haemoglobin to form carbaminohaemoglobin; CO2 reacts with terminal amine (-NH2) groups of globin chains; carbaminohaemoglobin dissociates in lungs / pulmonary circulation where $pCO_2$ low and $pO_2$ high, releasing CO2.

hints: Think where in the body $pO_2$ is highest and red cells are separated from air by only two very thin walls - tiny blood vessels wrapped tightly around air sacs.
walkthrough:
Link loading to high $pO_2$**
Haemoglobin loads oxygen where oxygen is plentiful and diffuses in. That is where deoxygenated blood is brought close to inspired air.

Pinpoint the vessels**
The precise site is the alveolar capillaries, the network around each alveolus in the lungs. Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air across the alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium into red cells to form oxyhaemoglobin.
Final answer: alveolar capillaries / capillaries surrounding alveoli in the lungs.

hints: Compare the two curves in Fig. 3.2 at the same $pO_2$, for example at 4 kPa or 6 kPa. Notice which curve is lower and which direction it has moved when 2,3-DPG increases.
Think how to quantify that change in affinity using $P_{50}$, the $pO_2$ needed for 50% saturation. Read off the $P_{50}$ for low and high 2,3-DPG from the graph.
walkthrough:
Describe the shift**
With high 2,3-DPG the whole curve lies to the right and lower. For example at $pO_2 = 4$ kPa, saturation is about 65% with low 2,3-DPG but only about 35% with high 2,3-DPG. So at every $pO_2$, haemoglobin is less saturated.

Use $P_{50}$ to show lower affinity**
$P_{50}$ is the $pO_2$ for 50% saturation. Reading across from 50% to each curve and down, $P_{50}$ rises from about 3.2 kPa (low 2,3-DPG) to about 4.6 kPa (high 2,3-DPG). A higher $P_{50}$ means lower affinity, so more $O_2$ is released.
Final answer: Curve shifts to the right / is lower; haemoglobin less saturated at any given $pO_2$ / higher $pO_2$ needed for same saturation; $P_{50}$ increases from about 3.2 kPa to about 4.6 kPa.

hints: Stored blood has lost 2,3-DPG, so decide which curve in Fig. 3.2 now applies - the left-hand low-DPG curve or the right-hand high-DPG curve - and what that means for holding onto oxygen.
Link that curve position to affinity and then to what happens in respiring tissues where $pO_2$ is low. Think whether oxygen will be released easily or held tightly.
walkthrough:
Apply low DPG to the graph**
Blood bank storage lowers 2,3-DPG, so haemoglobin follows the left-hand low-DPG curve. That curve shows higher saturation at tissue $pO_2$, meaning haemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly.

Explain the tissue effect**
Higher affinity means less dissociation in respiring tissues during an operation. Less oxygen is unloaded and made available for aerobic respiration, so oxygen supply to tissues is reduced.
Final answer: Less oxygen supplied to tissues; haemoglobin has higher affinity for oxygen so releases / unloads less oxygen.
